decisions.reason: The particle therapy water phantom is a high-investment flagship with a publicly announced Q1/2019 release, so withdrawing it now would write off substantial development costs and contradict a visible commitment.

Small-volume chambers are core to the firm's dosimetry heritage, need little ongoing cost once calibrated and certified, and any early weak results can be attributed to normal clinical adoption cycles.

Although it overlaps with Product B, the firm has publicly positioned it on its own page within its core chamber line, so dropping it within a year would expose the launch decision without a clear failure signal.
A standard clinical ionization chamber is a staple of the reference dosimetry portfolio tied to accredited calibration services, making withdrawal unlikely.
The relative dosimetry chamber complements the water phantom systems and the firm's integrated QA platform, so it supports the announced strategic direction.
Thimble chambers are a long-standing core product category with regulatory certification already invested, and there is no evidence yet that would justify abandoning it.
